peer_comps_note:
The supplied peer file names GoDaddy and Akamai as the closest proxies and concludes the valuation is "in line," reasoning that VeriSign's 26.7 times price-to-free-cash-flow is "broadly in line with what a durable, monopoly-like internet-infrastructure asset commands (comparable in spirit to Akamai's mid-teens or premium registrar/infra multiples)." That conclusion does not survive a live check of the peer multiples, which is exactly the stale-anchor trap: peer multiples de-rate, and an old anchor manufactures a discount that is not there.

Pulled live on 22 September 2026: GoDaddy trades at 9.5 times enterprise value to free cash flow, 11.6 times enterprise value to EBITDA and 3.2 times enterprise value to sales. Akamai trades at 19.4 times EBITDA and 5.8 times sales (its 39.7 times free-cash-flow multiple is a capital-spending artefact - capital expenditure is 18.9% of its revenue). VeriSign trades at 27.3 times enterprise value to free cash flow, 24.2 times EBITDA and 17.0 times sales. On the cleanest comparable line, EBITDA, VeriSign carries roughly a 25% premium to Akamai and more than double GoDaddy's multiple.

A large premium is correct here and the peer file's underlying logic is sound: GoDaddy is a competitive retailer and in fact VeriSign's own customer, with a fraction of the margin; Akamai is a capital-hungry content-delivery business with a 3.8% operating return on assets. VeriSign has an exclusive federal-contract monopoly, an 88.2% gross margin, a 67.9% operating margin and 2.1% capital intensity. The question is not whether the premium is deserved but whether this much premium is. Our base case of $298 implies about 20.4 times 2027 EBITDA - roughly where Akamai trades today, which is where we think a far better business belongs. The live price of $304.93 sits just above that. We also agree with the peer file on one important technical point: the deeply negative return on equity, return on invested capital and Altman-Z solvency score are artefacts of negative book equity created by a decade of buybacks, not evidence of operating weakness or distress, and the fair-value models in the scan that print a -100% margin of safety are broken by the same input.
interrogator_dossier:
# VeriSign (VRSN) — a deep dive on management and the setup

*Prepared 22 September 2026. Sources: five consecutive quarterly earnings calls (24 April 2025 through 23 July 2026), the screener's financial trajectory, balance-sheet and trailing-twelve-month data pulled live from Financial Modeling Prep on 22 September 2026, and dated company news through 21 September 2026. Share price used throughout: $304.93 (Nasdaq, US dollars, 22 September 2026).*

---

## 1. Narrative arc

VeriSign runs the official address book for every `.com` and `.net` web address. It sells only to accredited retailers — never to the public — and the price it may charge for `.com` is capped by a cooperative agreement with the US Department of Commerce. For most of the past decade the story management told was a simple one: a slowly shrinking or flat number of registered names, offset by contractual price increases, with all the surplus cash returned to shareholders. It was a utility that bought back its own stock.

Across these five calls that story changed materially, and in a specific order.

**April 2025 (first quarter 2025) — stabilisation.** The tone is defensive-to-neutral. Management leads with "sequentially improving trends and the soundness of our business model." The combined name base is 169.8 million, up 777,000 from year-end. New registrations are 10.1 million. The renewal rate is 75.3% against 74.1% a year earlier. The word doing the work is "improving" — from a low base.

**July and October 2025 — the marketing programmes arrive.** Management begins crediting a redesigned set of incentive programmes aimed at its retail channel. This is the first time in years the company claims it can *influence* volume rather than merely price it.

**February 2026 (fourth quarter 2025) — the inflection is named.** Management starts framing the volume recovery as durable rather than promotional.

**April 2026 (first quarter 2026) — the story becomes a growth story.** The name base hits a record 176.1 million. New registrations of 11.5 million are "the largest we have seen since the first half of 2021," up 14% year over year. The renewal rate rises to 76.3% from 75.5%. Management raises and narrows its 2026 name-base growth guidance to 3.1%–4.3%. Two new growth drivers are introduced in the same call: a price increase of $0.71 on the `.com` wholesale rate (from $10.26 to $10.97, effective 1 November 2026), and a teaser for unnamed security products to be revealed through a series of blog posts. Chief executive Jim Bidzos also introduces the artificial-intelligence tailwind explicitly: AI tools "make content and website creation faster and easier."

**July 2026 (second quarter 2026) — two step-changes at once.** New registrations reach a record 12.7 million, up 21% year over year. The name base reaches 179.1 million. Guidance for name-base growth is raised again, from 3.1%–4.3% to **5.2%–6.0%** — a near-doubling of the growth outlook inside one quarter. And on the night before the call the company announced that **`.web` has been delegated into the internet's root zone with VeriSign as registry operator**, ending roughly a decade of litigation and arbitration. Unlike `.com`, `.web` carries no price cap, allows premium-name sales, and requires only six months' notice to change wholesale pricing.

**What was quietly dropped and then restored.** In April 2026 management promised a blog series on new security products "starting as soon as next month." It did not appear. On the July call, unprompted, Bidzos addressed it: "We didn't put our new product efforts on hold… We simply paused the rollout of the blogs as we focused on resolving and delegating `.web`." The products have been "operational in test mode since early this year." This is a small, honest correction of a missed self-imposed deadline — handled better than most managements handle such things.

**Net arc:** from a price-and-buyback utility to a company claiming genuine volume growth, a brand-new untethered product line, and a security adjacency — inside five quarters.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials (forensic)

| Management claim | Where it holds | Where it diverges |
|---|---|---|
| "Strong results… both operationally and financially" (Q2 2026) | Revenue $435M, up 6.0% year over year; net income $217M; earnings per share $2.38, up 7.7%. Trailing-twelve-month revenue $1.71B, operating income $1.16B — a 67.9% operating margin. All real. | Earnings-per-share growth **decelerated** from +11.4% in the first quarter to +7.7% in the second. Operating-income growth decelerated from +8.3% to +5.6%. The financial trajectory is flattening even as the operating metrics accelerate. |
| Record new registrations, up 21% year over year | Verified in the transcript and consistent with the raised name-base guidance. The combined base did grow 3.05 million sequentially in the June quarter. | Revenue grew only 6.0% against 21% unit growth, because revenue is recognised evenly across the life of each one-year subscription and because the *base* — not the gross additions — drives revenue. Unit records are not revenue records. |
| Renewal rates are "solid" and the programmes produce "quality names" | The first-time renewal rate has held in "the mid-40% range for several quarters," and the previously-renewed rate is "in the mid-80% range." Both are consistent with history. | The reported renewal rate **fell** year over year in the June quarter: 75.2% against 75.5%. The chief financial officer conceded the decline will continue — "we still have some expectation there in the remainder of this year and then possibly into next year." A mid-40% first-time renewal rate means roughly 55% of that record 12.7-million cohort is expected to disappear within a year. |
| The growth is structural, driven by AI and by our own marketing | Plausible and management is candid that it cannot decompose the two: "taking it all apart, parsing it out in detail, difficult." | **The volume is being bought.** Second-quarter operating expense was $138M against $121M a year earlier — up roughly 14%, against revenue up 6.0%. Operating leverage ran backwards this quarter. That is the price of the incentive programmes, and it is the single most important number on the call that management did not highlight. |
| Capital returns exceed cash generation | Confirmed: $1.17B returned over the trailing twelve months against trailing free cash flow of $1.07B — more than 100%, funded partly by borrowing. Buyback authorisation topped up by $884M to $1.5B. Quarterly dividend $0.81. | The balance sheet shows the cost. Shareholders' equity is **negative $2.25B** at 30 June 2026 — years of buying back stock above book value. Net debt is $1.31B (borrowings $2.33B plus $6M of leases, less $1.03B of cash and short-term investments). This is a liability, not a cash cushion. |
| Guidance raised twice in 2026 | Revenue guidance moved from $1.730–1.745B (April) to $1.745–1.755B (July); operating income from $1.170–1.185B to $1.185–1.195B. Both raises are real and modest. | The revenue raise was roughly $12M at the midpoint — about 0.7%. The name-base growth guidance nearly doubled. The gap between the volume raise and the revenue raise is the ratable-recognition lag, and it is the mechanical reason unit enthusiasm should not be capitalised at a growth multiple today. |

**On the headline return figures in the screener.** Return on equity of −47% and return on invested capital of −12,213% are arithmetic artefacts of negative book equity and negative invested capital (−$351M on a trailing basis), not signs of a broken business. The same applies to the Altman-Z solvency score of −2.2 and to the fair-value models that print a −100% margin of safety: a discounted-cash-flow or earnings-power model fed negative equity produces nonsense. The honest returns statement is simpler — this company earns roughly $1.07B of free cash on about $228M of net property and $65M or less of annual capital spending. Capital intensity is 2.1% of revenue. The economics are outstanding; the *accounting* capital base has been bought away.

---

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Rising, and measurably so.**

- *April 2025:* hedged and incremental — "sequentially improving trends."
- *April 2026:* confident and quantified — new registrations "the largest we have seen since the first half of 2021"; guidance raised.
- *July 2026:* the most assertive language in the series — "a record 12.7 million new registrations," "the largest we have seen for any quarter in our history," "the first quarter renewal rate is the highest rate we have seen in 20 years." Bidzos reaches for the word "convergence" to describe the AI and channel tailwinds stacking, and says explicitly: "I called that if I didn't use the word convergence, I should have. I'll use it now."

The language moved from defensive (efficiency, stability, uptime) to offensive (records, marketing investment, new products, a new top-level domain). Importantly, the confidence is attached to *volume* metrics, not to earnings. Management has never once claimed an earnings inflection. That restraint is to their credit and is also the tell: they are describing a better business, not yet a faster-compounding one.

One genuinely defensive note appears in July 2026, on capital spending. The chief financial officer says server and memory prices "had a meaningful impact on our business," that the company pulled spending forward "to avoid price increases that we know are coming in the upcoming six months," and that prices will "probably be more elevated" next year because "we're competing with a lot of data centre capacity that's trying to be built right now." Bidzos then overrides the cost concern outright: "regardless of what the market price for the technology… we will simply make that investment… without hesitation." That is the correct answer for an infrastructure operator and a modest negative for 2027 margins.

---

## 4. Guidance credibility

**High.**

The record here is unusually clean because VeriSign gives narrow, mechanical guidance and then does not touch it mid-quarter.

- 2026 name-base growth: guided, then raised in April (3.1%–4.3%), then raised again in July (5.2%–6.0%). Both raises were supported by disclosed unit data that anyone can verify daily on the company's own website — management points investors there explicitly. That is the opposite of sandbagging by obscurity.
- 2026 revenue: $1.730–1.745B in April → $1.745–1.755B in July. Delivered against, not walked back.
- Operating income, capital spending and tax-rate guidance were all reaffirmed or narrowed, never cut.
- The second-quarter print beat the consensus estimate ($2.38 against $2.36).

The screener's beat rate of four in seven quarters (57%) looks middling but reflects how tightly this company is modelled — the misses are pennies on a business with no demand surprise, not credibility failures.

The single best credibility marker in the set is the chief financial officer's unprompted, precise explanation of how the November price increase flows through: a name renewing on 30 October 2027 sees no increase until then, "you could really think about the price increase as it relates to our existing base, takes two years to really flow through revenue completely," and "we would expect about 50% of November's 7% price increase on `.com` to be recognised in 2027 revenues, the rest… 2028." Managements running a promotional narrative do not volunteer the two-year delay on their own good news.

**Reliability: High.**

---

## 5. Analyst pressure points

Four questions recur, and management's answers tell you where the uncertainty actually sits.

1. **Is the registration surge a pull-forward ahead of the November price increase?** Asked in both the April and July calls. Bidzos: "I can't say that's not a factor. It could be a factor for some registrations. We just don't see it as anything coming close to a material factor." That is a careful non-denial. The record 12.7-million quarter ended four months before the increase took effect, and registrars can lock a year of wholesale pricing by registering early. This is unresolved and it is the most important open question in the file.

2. **What happens to churn when the record cohorts come up for renewal?** Citi pushed directly on this in July. The answer was honest but not reassuring: yes, the renewal rate will tick down; we think our programmes offset some of it. The renewal rate has already fallen year over year.

3. **What is `.web` actually worth?** Two analysts pressed on go-to-market and on cost. Management gave a clear process timeline (90 days of security testing, then a minimum 30-day trademark-holders window, then an optional limited-registration period in which every existing `.com` holder may claim the matching `.web`, then general availability "late this year or very, very early next year") and clear structural advantages (no price cap, premium names allowed, marketing freedom). It gave **no** pricing, **no** volume expectation, and **no** revenue contribution — "at this time, we don't expect meaningful revenue or expenses related to `.web` for 2026."

4. **What are the new security products?** Asked three times across two calls. The answers are directionally consistent (public-key infrastructure heritage, zero-trust, agentic-AI security, runs on the existing infrastructure) and commercially empty. No product name, no pricing, no launch date, no addressable market.

A topic analysts pushed on that *did* turn into news: the missed blog-series deadline from April, which management pre-emptively addressed in July.

A topic analysts did **not** push on, and should have: the 14% year-over-year rise in operating expense against 6% revenue growth. Not one question on the second-quarter call asked what the incentive programmes cost or what return they earn.

---

## 6. Red flags and green flags

🔴 **Operating leverage reversed in the June quarter.** Revenue +6.0%, operating expense +14%, operating income +5.6%. Growth is being purchased.

🔴 **The renewal rate declined year over year** (75.2% against 75.5%) and the chief financial officer guided it lower "in the remainder of this year and then possibly into next year." A mid-40% first-time renewal rate means most of the record new-registration cohort is expected to lapse.

🔴 **Insiders are selling, decisively.** Two open-market purchases totalling 19 shares against 76 sales totalling 50,200 shares. Chief executive Bidzos sold 3,300 shares for roughly $979,000 on 13 August 2026. The screener's insider buy-ratio field is inflated by share grants and should be ignored.

🔴 **A new antitrust class action.** On 2 September 2026 the law firm Hagens Berman announced a class action against VeriSign and ICANN alleging an unlawful monopoly and excessive `.com` fees. The company's structural defence is strong — its `.com` price is a ceiling *set by* a federal cooperative agreement with the Department of Commerce, not a price it chose — but this is a new, unquantified legal overhang on the single asset that produces essentially all the profit.

🔴 **Negative book equity of $2.25B and $1.31B of net debt**, with more than 100% of free cash flow returned over the trailing year. There is no balance-sheet cushion; the company is a going-concern cash machine with no asset floor beneath it.

🔴 **Rising capital-spending prices.** Management says server and memory costs will be "more elevated" in 2027 and that it will buy regardless of price.

🟢 **Volume genuinely inflected.** Record 12.7 million new registrations, up 21% year over year, a record 179.1-million name base, and a guidance raise from 3.1%–4.3% to 5.2%–6.0% in a single quarter. Whatever the cause, the units are real and independently verifiable daily.

🟢 **`.web` was won and delegated on 22 July 2026**, after roughly a decade of disputes. It carries no price cap, allows premium-name sales, and can be marketed freely — three freedoms `.com` does not have. It is a genuine free option: zero registrations today, and the company can offer it to every one of its ~166 million `.com` holders first.

🟢 **A dated, contractual price increase is already noticed.** `.com` wholesale moves from $10.26 to $10.97 on 1 November 2026 — roughly 6.9%, on a base of about 166 million names, at close to 100% incremental margin, with about half recognised in 2027 and the rest in 2028.

🟢 **Twenty-nine consecutive years of 100% service availability**, roughly 600 billion daily transactions, and "multiple orders of magnitude" of spare capacity. The operational moat is not a slogan.

🟢 **Quality scores corroborate the franchise:** Piotroski 9 of 9, gross margin 88.2% and stable, net margin 49.8%, free-cash-flow margin 64.5%, capital spending 2.1% of revenue.

---

## 7. Hidden signals

**A vocabulary shift from reliability to security.** Across 2025 the differentiator management named was availability — uptime, resilience, root-server operation. From April 2026 the phrase becomes "high assurance," deliberately defined to bundle availability *plus* cryptographic accuracy *plus* millisecond latency *plus* spare capacity. This is the language of a company preparing to sell a second product into the same infrastructure. Bidzos ties it to agentic AI: "the security challenge with AI will be met by sharpening and hardening the tools… in pursuit of compliance with something called the Zero Trust principles."

**AI is framed as a demand driver, not a threat — and management never once addresses the inverse.** The bear argument on this business is that AI answer engines and agents reduce the need for a branded website, and therefore for a domain name. No analyst asked it directly and management never volunteered it. What management did volunteer is the counter-argument, which is decent: the DNS is the unique, stable, globally governed identifier that agents themselves must resolve, and "alternate name spaces don't really have what the DNS has." Note that the evidence is currently entirely on management's side — registrations are at records.

**A chief financial officer transition completed cleanly.** George Kilguss retired in May 2025; John Calys stepped up from global controller. Calys's disclosure style is, if anything, more mechanically precise than his predecessor's — the unprompted two-year price-flow-through explanation is the example.

**`.net` pricing is an unpulled lever.** Bidzos: "we have available 10% annual price increases on `.net`. We don't guide to pricing… we have not at this point announced a price increase for `.net`." A second, smaller, entirely discretionary price lever sits unused.

**A telling omission on `.web` pricing.** Asked repeatedly, management said only "we have nothing to say about `.web` pricing today. We're still working on that," while noting that "compared to [other top-level domains], `.com` is a very low-priced" one. The hint is that `.web` will be priced well above $10.97. That is upside nobody can model yet — including management.

---

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict

**Trajectory: STRENGTHENING.** The operating business is demonstrably better than it was five quarters ago: records in the name base and in new registrations, guidance raised twice, a decade-long legal dispute resolved in the company's favour, a dated price increase in hand, a second price lever unused, and a security adjacency in test. Credibility is high and the disclosure is unusually clean.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing.** The volume inflection is real but it has not yet reached the earnings line, and in the most recent quarter it moved the earnings line the *wrong* way — operating expense up roughly 14% against revenue up 6.0%, operating-income growth decelerating from 8.3% to 5.6%. Roughly 55% of the record new-registration cohort is expected to lapse at first renewal, the renewal rate has already ticked down, and management cannot rule out that some of the surge was pulled forward ahead of the 1 November price increase. The market has already paid for the structural interpretation: the stock is 96% of the way up its 52-week range, about 46% above its 52-week low of $208.86 and roughly 17% above its 200-day average, at about 32 times this year's expected earnings and roughly 27 times enterprise value to free cash flow. The question for a buyer at $304.93 is not whether this is a great business — it plainly is — but whether an inflection that has so far produced 7.7% earnings growth deserves a growth multiple.

**Economic moat: WIDE, of the regulatory-licence type, reinforced by scale-cost and by a genuine operational intangible.** VeriSign holds an exclusive contract to operate `.com` and `.net`, priced by a ceiling set in a federal cooperative agreement. Nobody can enter. The evidence of width is in the margins and the capital intensity: 88.2% gross margin (stable), 67.9% trailing operating margin, 64.5% free-cash-flow margin, capital spending at 2.1% of revenue, and 29 unbroken years of perfect availability that no competitor can retroactively acquire.

**Moat trend: STABLE, not widening.** Margins are near their historical peak (the screener puts the margin roughly 1.1 standard deviations above its own history) and the June quarter's cost step-up, together with the flagged 2027 hardware inflation and the declining renewal rate, argues against calling it wider. The unique constraint on this moat is that it is a *capped* monopoly: the licence prevents competition and simultaneously prevents VeriSign from charging what the asset is worth. `.web` is the first meaningful escape from that cap in the company's history, and it is exactly why `.web` matters more than its likely near-term revenue.

**Secular threat: MANAGEABLE.** The plausible terminal risk is that AI answer engines and autonomous agents erode the need for a human-navigable branded web address. Today the evidence points the other way — management attributes a 21% year-over-year jump in new registrations partly to AI tools lowering the cost of building a site, and the DNS remains the identifier agents themselves must resolve. This is a risk to monitor over a decade, not a force visibly compressing the base. The cheapness question is therefore moot in the other direction: this is not a fear-print and it is not a value trap. It is a high-quality franchise at a price that already reflects a good outcome.

Management credibility 5 of 5 · trajectory improving · a wide, durable moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.

bull_thesis: VeriSign is a toll road on the internet's address book. It is the only operator of .com and .net, which together hold 179.1 million names as of June 2026. It keeps 88 cents of each revenue dollar as gross profit and turns about 64% of revenue into free cash flow (the cash left after running and maintaining the business). The bull case is that growth is shifting up a gear and the market still prices VeriSign as a 5%-a-year compounder. In the second quarter of 2026 new registrations hit a record 12.7 million, up 21% on the year. That followed a 14% gain in the first quarter and a 76.3% renewal rate, the highest in 20 years. Management raised its 2026 name-count growth guide twice, to 5.2%-6.0%. Three layers of growth are now stacking. First, the name count itself is rising 5-6%. Second, the $0.71 (6.9%) .com wholesale price increase takes effect on 2026-11-01. The CFO said about half of it shows up in 2027 revenue and the rest in 2028, and it falls almost entirely to profit. Third, the share count shrinks about 2.5-3% a year, because more than 100% of free cash flow goes back to shareholders. The trailing twelve-month return was $1.17B, and the buyback authorization was refilled to $1.5B on 2026-07-23. Put together, earnings per share could compound at 10-12% through 2028: about $9.50 in 2026 and about $10.60 in 2027 on our estimates. Two free options sit on top. One is .web, the company's first top-level domain with unregulated pricing and premium-name sales, with general availability expected late 2026 or early 2027. The other is a set of security services built on the same infrastructure. Management credibility is high: every 2026 guide was raised, not cut. The negative return-on-capital and solvency scores are accounting artifacts of buybacks, not distress. Conditions for the bull case: new-registration cohorts keep renewing at the historic first-time rate (mid-40%); the November price increase does not trigger a registrar-led drop in renewals; and regulators leave the pre-set .com price-increase allowances in place.
bear_thesis: The business is excellent. The bear case is about price and a few fresh risks. At $276.43 the stock trades at about 30 times trailing earnings per share of $9.22, about 25 times trailing free cash flow, and about 17 times trailing gross profit on an enterprise-value basis (enterprise value = market value plus net debt of about $1.3B). That is a full multiple for a company whose revenue has grown about 5-6% a year for five years and whose five-year earnings-per-share growth is only about 5.9% a year. First, the 2026 registration surge may be partly borrowed. It arrived just before a publicly announced price increase, and management only says pull-forward is 'not close to a material factor', without numbers. The renewal rate already slipped to an expected 75.2% in the second quarter from 75.5% a year earlier, and management expects further small declines as young, promotion-driven names come up for renewal. If the first renewals of the 2025-26 cohorts disappoint in 2027, growth reverts to the 2-3% of recent years just as the market has priced in 5-6%. Second, the pricing moat is a regulatory privilege. On 2026-09-04 Hagens Berman filed an antitrust class action against VeriSign and ICANN alleging excessive .com fees. Past challenges have not changed the model, but this one adds legal cost and headline risk. It could also give political cover to anyone who wants to freeze the price-increase allowance. Third, costs are rising: second-quarter operating expenses rose to $138M from $121M a year earlier, and management calls server-memory price inflation 'meaningful' for capital spending. Fourth, insiders only sell: 78 open-market sales against 2 token purchases. The chief executive has sold 3,300 shares roughly monthly near $305. Fifth, .web and the security products have no disclosed pricing or revenue targets, and .web revenue will build slowly because it is recognized over each registration's term. What would confirm the bear case: name-count growth tracking below 4% after November 1; a renewal rate falling below 74%; any regulator move on .com pricing; or a de-rating of quality compounders toward 22-24 times earnings.
consensus_delta: Viewed as a value situation, the question is whether the street is pricing terminal decline into a company whose earnings are stable or growing. It is not. The street is pricing VeriSign as a high-quality compounder, and we largely agree. The few price targets are thin but uniformly positive: Wedbush at $341 (2026-09-01) and $324 (2026-07-24), and Baird at $355 (2026-04-24). Consensus is $348, and only two targets were published in the last quarter, so this is not a street-wide view. Those targets assume the 5-6% name-count growth of 2026 carries into 2027-28 on top of the price increase, which implies roughly 30 times 2027 earnings. Where we differ: we think 2026 unit growth partly reflects buying ahead of the known November price increase, plus a cohort of promotion-driven names whose first renewal is still ahead. So we underwrite 4-5% name-count growth for 2027, not 6%, and a lower multiple of about 22.5 times forward operating profit. That gives $300, about 14% below the street average. The market price of $276 sits below both. The market has already discounted some of this, which is why the stock is now interesting rather than rich. It is not yet cheap.
forcing_function: No single event forces a re-rating. The value closes through compounding. The dated checkpoints are: (1) the third-quarter 2026 report in late October 2026, which will give a registration and renewal read ahead of the price increase; (2) the .com wholesale increase to $10.97 on 2026-11-01, which lifts 2027-28 revenue by about 7% on .com, with about half landing in 2027; (3) .web general availability, expected late 2026 or early 2027, which is the first sign of whether premium-name and unregulated pricing can build a second revenue line; (4) the fourth-quarter report in early February 2027, with first 2027 guidance; and (5) the planned rollout of security services. Continuing buybacks, $1.5B authorized as of 2026-07-23 and about 6% of market value, retire shares at any price, so intrinsic value per share rises about 10-11% a year regardless.
valley_of_death: No forced event threatens the business before the value gap closes. There are no refinancing walls: the 2027 notes were redeemed on 2026-07-20 with 5.1% notes due 2031. There is no cash burn, and the company generates about $1.07B of free cash flow a year. The risky window is the next three to nine months, driven by data. (1) The third-quarter report in late October 2026 will show whether new registrations held up in the last full quarter before the price increase. (2) November-December 2026 registration and renewal data will show how buyers respond after the increase and whether a pull-forward hangover appears. Management already expects the renewal rate to tick down. (3) The antitrust class action filed 2026-09-04 moves to motions, which brings headline risk. (4) Server-memory cost inflation may push 2027 capital spending up; management has declined to guide 2027. A de-rating of quality compounders, from 30 times toward 24 times earnings, would cost about 20% with no change in the business. That is the main path to our $220 adverse case.
positioning_washout: There is limited risk of forced selling. The dividend is well covered, since it is a small part of a cash return that exceeds 100% of free cash flow, so no dividend cut will flush income holders. The shareholder base is concentrated in index funds and long-only holders; BlackRock disclosed about 9.3% (August 2026 filing reports). Berkshire Hathaway is a long-standing large holder that reduced its stake in 2025; a further Berkshire sale is the one lump that could weigh on the price. Insider supply is steady but small: the chief executive sells 3,300 shares roughly monthly out of about 385,000, and there were 78 open-market insider sales against 2 token buys. The smart-money and institutional-flow scores in our data are neutral (51 out of 100). A 9% slide in the past week with no company news looks like rotation out of defensive quality names rather than a washout. There is no mechanical seller large enough to force a capitulation price.
moderator_conclusion: Watchlist, not a buy yet. This is a wonderful business at a fair price that is edging toward a good one. Since our last look nothing in the business has changed. The second-quarter results on 2026-07-23 were strong, .web is delegated, the 6.9% .com price increase takes effect on 2026-11-01, and there is a new antitrust suit dated 2026-09-04. The stock, however, has fallen about 9%, from $304.93 to $276.43. Our parts-based fair value is about $300. The core registry is worth about $27.9B at 22.5 times forward operating profit, .web adds a small $0.4B option, and $1.3B of net debt comes off. That puts the stock roughly 8% below fair value, against about 2% above it last time. We move the name from pass to watchlist and nudge conviction from 2 to 3. We stop short of a buy for three reasons. The margin of safety is thin. The downside to our adverse case ($220, about 20% below) outweighs the upside to fair value (about 8.5%). And the next two quarters directly test the one claim we cannot verify: that the record 2026 registrations were not borrowed from after the November price increase. Level we are waiting for: about $245 or lower, where the stock would trade near 23 times 2027 estimated earnings and at least 18% below fair value. Alternatively, a clean third-quarter report and November-December data showing renewals holding near 75% and name-count growth staying above 4% after the increase. Either could lift fair value to about $320 and justify buying nearer today's price. The regime backdrop adds no push either way. The thesis does not depend on rate cuts, oil or AI capital spending; artificial intelligence here helps demand for domain names rather than acting as a shared macro bet. So we apply no regime tilt. The value score is 3 out of 5. The moat is wide and stable, the forensics are clean and management is highly credible, but the discount to fair value is too small for a higher score.
sop_fair_value: $300 per share (base case), against a live price of $276.43 - about 8% below fair value.
sop_breakdown: Base case on about 90.3 million diluted shares. (1) The .com/.net registry: next-twelve-month operating profit of about $1.24B, at the midpoint of 2026 guidance ($1.185-$1.195B) plus the early flow-through of the November price increase. At 22.5 times that is $27.9B. The multiple works out to roughly 17.5 times forward gross profit, the house enterprise-value-to-gross-profit method, against about 17.4 times today on trailing figures. It is also roughly 27 times 2027 estimated earnings per share of $10.60. (2) .web: $0.4B, a modest option value for the only unregulated-pricing top-level domain in the portfolio. (3) Security services: zero. (4) Less net debt of $1.30B, excluding leases. The $6M of capitalized leases is immaterial. Total: about $27.0B, or $300 per share. risk_reward: From $276.43, the adverse case of $220 is about 20% below and the base case of $300 is about 8.5% above; the favorable case is $362. The downside to the adverse case is more than twice the upside to fair value. There is no structural floor: VeriSign has net debt, not net cash. The underlying value grows about 10-11% a year through buybacks and earnings, so holding costs little. But the entry price does not yet offer a margin of safety.
peer_comps_note: The peer file groups VeriSign with GoDaddy (a registrar that resells VeriSign's names at retail) and Cloudflare (network security, much faster growth). interrogator_dossier:
# VeriSign (VRSN) - a deep dive on management and the setup

As of 2026-09-29. Live price used: $276.43 (US dollars, Nasdaq listing), fetched from the FMP quote feed today. Transcripts reviewed: Q1 2025 (2025-04-24) through Q1 2026 (2026-04-23) from the bundled file, plus the Q2 2026 call (2026-07-23) pulled live from FMP because it post-dates the bundle.

Bottom line: this is one of the most credible management teams we cover. For six straight calls the story and the numbers have moved together, and in 2026 the numbers moved ahead of the story - guidance for growth in the .com and .net name count was raised twice, from roughly flat-to-slightly-up in early 2025 to 5.2%-6.0% for 2026. The questions are no longer about honesty. They are about how much of the recent surge in new registrations is durable, and how much of this good news the share price already carries.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

- **Early 2025 (Q1 2025): recovery and a new dividend.** The call opened on a business emerging from two years of a shrinking name count. Management flagged "improving domain name-based trends" in all three main regions, raised name-count guidance, but kept "a measure of caution until the macroeconomic situation clarifies." The headline was the first-ever quarterly dividend (77 cents), framed as a "natural evolutionary step" that "doesn't change the way we think about the total amount of shareholder return." It was also the handover call from long-time CFO George Kilguss to John Calys.
- **Mid-to-late 2025 (Q2-Q3 2025): momentum confirmed.** Guidance moved from a slight decline to positive growth, then higher again. The buyback authorization was topped up. The long .web dispute was discussed only defensively - "an abusive process ... pursued in bad faith" by the rival bidder.
- **Year-end 2025 (Q4 call, 2026-02-05):** the name base grew by 4.5 million names (about 2.6%) in 2025 to 173.5 million, and more than $1.1 billion went back to shareholders. Management hinted at the October-2026 window for a .com wholesale price increase while refusing to guide on it.
- **Q1 2026 (2026-04-23): offense.** A record 176.1 million names, the most new registrations since early 2021, a renewal rate of 76.3% (the highest in 20 years), guidance raised to 3.1%-4.3%, and formal notice of a 71-cent (6.9%) .com wholesale price increase, from $10.26 to $10.97, effective November 1, 2026. A new theme appeared: security products built on the company's "high assurance" infrastructure, with artificial intelligence cast as both a demand driver and a source of new security needs.
- **Q2 2026 (2026-07-23): the strongest quarter in the company's history on unit metrics.** A record 12.7 million new registrations (up 21% on the year), a name base of 179.1 million, name-count guidance raised again to 5.2%-6.0%, revenue guidance raised to $1.745-$1.755 billion and operating-income guidance to $1.185-$1.195 billion. The day before, .web was finally delegated into the internet root with VeriSign as operator, "following the successful resolution of all previous disputes." A fresh $884 million was added to the buyback, bringing the authorization back to $1.5 billion.

The arc runs from "defensive recovery" to "accelerating growth plus two new options" (.web and security services). Nothing was quietly dropped; the security-products launch was delayed for a quarter while .web was resolved, and management said so plainly.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Name-base trends are improving and accelerating | Revenue rose from $1.49B (2023) to $1.56B (2024) to $1.66B (2025); quarterly revenue went $419M (Q3 2025), $425M, $429M, $435M (Q2 2026), about 6% a year | Matches. Revenue growth lags unit growth because revenue is recognized evenly over each registration's life. |
| Operating leverage - a slight improvement in operating margin | Operating margin about 67.8% in Q3 2025, 68.4% in Q1 2026, 68.2% in Q2 2026; gross margin steady near 88% | Matches, modestly. Q2 operating costs rose to $138M from $121M a year ago (marketing programs, and server-memory price inflation on capital spending). |
| More than 100% of free cash flow returned to shareholders | $1.17B returned in the twelve months to June 2026 against trailing free cash flow of about $1.07B; diluted share count fell from 93.6M (Q3 2025) to 91.1M (Q2 2026) | Matches. Funded partly by debt, which is why net debt is about $1.3B. |
| Earnings growth is double-digit | Diluted earnings per share (EPS) grew 11.4% in Q1 2026 and 7.7% in Q2 2026; trailing EPS $9.22; five-year EPS growth only about 5.9% a year because 2022 was a down year | Mostly matches recently; the long-run record is slower than the recent run. |
| Pull-forward ahead of the November price increase is "not close to a material factor" | Cannot be tested yet. New registrations rose 14% and 21% year on year in the last two quarters, right before a known price rise | Unproven. This is the single claim the next two quarters will test. |
| First-time renewals of the new cohort are holding in the mid-40% range | Overall renewal rate was 76.3% in Q1 2026 but slipped to an expected 75.2% in Q2 2026, versus 75.5% a year earlier | Partly matches. Management itself expects a further small tick down as young names become a bigger share of renewals. |

Balance-sheet notes. Reported return on invested capital and return on equity are negative, and the Altman-Z solvency score is -2.4. These are accounting artifacts of negative book equity created by decades of buybacks, not signs of distress; the business converts about 64% of revenue into free cash flow. Debt is modest against roughly $1.2B of annual operating income: $550M of 2027 notes were refinanced in June-July 2026 with 5.1% notes due 2031.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

Rating: Rising.
- Q1 2025: cautious - "a measure of caution until the macroeconomic situation clarifies."
- Q2 2025: guarded optimism - guidance reflects "positive momentum but continues to reflect some conservatism."
- Q3 2025: confident - "finishing out 2025 from a position of strength."
- Q1 2026: offensive - "The positive domain name base trends of 2025 have continued to build strength."
- Q2 2026: the most confident in years - "the factors driving the solid domain name base trends ... accelerated," with talk of a "synergistic convergence" of artificial-intelligence tailwinds and registrar customer-acquisition focus.

Guidance has become more specific over time (ranges narrowed as they rose). The shift is from defensive language to growth and new-product language, which is appropriate given the numbers, but it also means expectations are now higher.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

Every name-count guide in this window was raised, not cut: from a small decline in early 2025, to positive, to about 2.6% actual for 2025; then 3.1%-4.3% (April 2026) and 5.2%-6.0% (July 2026). Revenue and operating-income guidance were raised in both 2026 calls. The earnings-beat rate in our data is only 4 of 7 quarters, but the misses are pennies against analyst estimates, not against company guidance. There is a mild sandbagging pattern - early-year guides are set conservatively and raised as the year unfolds. Reliability: High.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **Pull-forward before the price rise.** Asked directly in Q2 2026; the answer ("could be a factor for some registrations ... nothing close to a material factor") is honest but unquantified.
- **Price elasticity and renewals after November 1.** Management defers to what retail registrars do with their own prices.
- **Cohort quality.** Analysts keep probing whether promotion-driven registrations will renew. Management answers with first-time renewal rates but does not disclose cohort detail.
- **.web economics.** No pricing, no revenue expectation for 2026, "very, very minimum" marketing spend. Revenue will build slowly because it is recognized over the registration term.
- **New security products.** Repeatedly teased ("you won't have to wait too much longer") with no pricing, revenue target, or customer data. Treat as an option with no value until launched.
- **Capital spending.** Server-memory price inflation is "meaningful"; some 2027 spend was pulled into 2026.

Not addressed by management on the calls: the antitrust class action filed on 2026-09-04 by Hagens Berman against VeriSign and ICANN (the internet's naming regulator) alleging excessive .com fees. It post-dates the Q2 call.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

Green flags
- Record new registrations (Q2 2026, 12.7 million) and a 20-year-high renewal rate (Q1 2026, 76.3%).
- Name-count guidance raised twice in 2026 (April and July).
- .web resolved and delegated (2026-07-22) after a dispute that dates back to 2016.
- 29 years of uninterrupted availability for .com and .net resolution.
- Share count shrinking about 2.5-3% a year; dividend raised from 77 to 81 cents.

Red flags
- Renewal rate slipping (75.2% expected for Q2 2026 versus 75.5% a year earlier), with management guiding to further small declines as young names mix in.
- A known November 1 price increase sits right after the registration surge - some of the surge may be pulled forward.
- Steady insider selling: 78 open-market sales (49,700 shares) versus 2 tiny purchases; the chief executive has been selling 3,300 shares roughly monthly (for example on 2026-08-11 and 2026-09-22 near $305), which looks like a pre-planned program but is not a vote of confidence.
- A new antitrust class action (2026-09-04). Past challenges to the .com pricing arrangement have not dented the model, but it adds headline and legal-cost risk.
- Operating expenses up about 14% year on year in Q2 2026, faster than revenue.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- The word "high assurance" has become a recurring frame since Q1 2026, and security products are being positioned for an "agentic AI" world. That is new language for a company that has sold one product for two decades; it signals a desire for a second growth leg.
- On .web, management stresses "complete wholesale pricing flexibility" and the ability to sell premium names - both impossible in .com. This is the most interesting strategic statement in the window: .web is the company's only unregulated pricing asset.
- The new CFO (John Calys, from May 2025) is more granular than his predecessor - for example, disclosing that about half of the November price increase will appear in 2027 revenue and the rest in 2028.
- The dividend was explicitly framed as not changing total shareholder return - so buybacks will absorb less cash at the margin, but total cash returned still exceeds free cash flow.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

Trajectory: strengthening. The name base is growing at its fastest rate in years, pricing power is being used within its regulatory cap, and nearly all cash is returned to shareholders.

The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: the business is not in question, the price is. At $276 the shares trade at about 30 times trailing earnings and about 25 times trailing free cash flow. Almost all of the good news - accelerating units, the 6.9% .com price rise, .web - is visible and widely modeled. The edge, if any, comes from buying below fair value, not from discovering something the market has missed.

Moat. The moat is a regulatory license: VeriSign is the sole operator of .com and .net under agreements with ICANN and a cooperative agreement with the US Department of Commerce, with pre-set price-increase allowances. It is wide: gross margin has held near 88%, operating margin has edged up to about 68%, and free-cash-flow margin is about 64%. The negative return on capital is a buyback artifact, not erosion. The trend is stable - the regulatory cap limits how fast the moat can widen, and nothing in the numbers shows it narrowing.

Secular threat. The obvious candidate is artificial intelligence replacing web navigation (answer engines reducing the need for a memorable address). The evidence so far runs the other way: management credits AI website-building tools for the registration surge, and the name base is at a record. The other structural risk is regulatory - a political or legal push to cap or cut .com pricing, now sharpened by the September 2026 antitrust suit. Both are real but manageable; neither shows up in the numbers today. The cheapness question does not arise - this is not a cheap stock - so this is neither a fear-print nor a value trap; it is a fairly priced quality compounder.

# VeriSign (VRSN) — a deep dive on management and the setup

*Committee continuing coverage. Prepared 2026-10-05. Live price $291.70 (NASDAQ, US dollars, FMP quote 2026-10-05). Evidence base: six earnings calls from Q1 2025 (2025-04-24) through Q2 2026 (2026-07-23; the Q2 2026 call was pulled from FMP because the bundled transcript file stops at Q1 2026), plus the screener's financial trajectory and dated news through 2026-10-01.*

**Takeaway up front:** VeriSign is a toll road on the internet's address book. It runs the .com and .net registries — a near-monopoly governed by a government contract — and turns roughly 64 cents of every revenue dollar into free cash flow (cash left after running the business and investing in it). Over the six quarters reviewed, management has done the rarest thing in this industry: it under-promised and then raised guidance every single quarter, as the base of registered names went from flat to growing about 5% a year. The story and the numbers agree. The only real questions are price (the stock trades close to what the business is worth) and regulation (a new antitrust class action filed 2026-09-04).

---

## 1. Narrative arc

**Early 2025 — "stabilization."** In Q1 2025 the message was defensive: the domain-name base had been shrinking through 2023–24, and management guided 2025 base growth to a range of "negative 0.7% … and positive 0.9%", explicitly carrying "a measure of caution until the macroeconomic situation clarifies." The upside talking points were narrow: registrars (the retail sellers such as GoDaddy) were "shifting towards customer acquisition" and engaging with VeriSign's marketing programs.

**Late 2025 — "recovery confirmed."** By Q4 2025 (call of 2026-02-05) the base had grown 2.6% for the year to 173.5 million names, new registrations hit 41.7 million (the most since 2021), a quarterly dividend begun in 2025 was raised 5.2%, and 2026 base growth was guided at 1.5–3.5%. Two new threads appeared: AI ("certainly having some impact, but it's one of several components") and unnamed "new services" in security.

**2026 — "acceleration plus optionality."** Q1 2026 (2026-04-23) brought a record 176.1 million names, the highest renewal rate in 20 years, and the announcement of a .com wholesale price rise to $10.97 effective 2026-11-01 (about 6.9%). Q2 2026 (2026-07-23) was the strongest call in the set: a record 12.7 million new registrations (up 21% year over year), base guidance raised and narrowed to 5.2–6.0%, .web finally delegated into the root zone (2026-07-22) after a decade of disputes, and a buyback authorization topped up to $1.5 billion.

**What was quietly de-emphasized:** the macro caution of 2025 disappeared entirely; the "new security services" were promised "in the coming months" in February, then paused behind .web in Q2 ("we simply paused the rollout"). That product line has now slipped twice in tone, though not in any formal guidance.

## 2. Claims vs financials (forensic)

| Management claim | Evidence in the numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Sound financial discipline" | Gross margin 88% (stable); operating margin ~68% (2025 operating income $1.12B on $1.66B revenue); net margin ~50% | Matches |
| Domain trends drive "profitable growth" | Revenue +6.4% in 2025, Q1 2026 +6.6%, Q2 2026 +6.0%; EPS (earnings per share) 2025 +10.1%, TTM (trailing twelve months) diluted EPS $9.22 | Matches; EPS growth outruns revenue because of buybacks |
| Returning ">100% of free cash flow" | TTM free cash flow ~$1.07B; $1.17B returned in the 12 months to Q2 2026 via buybacks and dividends | Matches — and it is funded partly by debt (see below) |
| "Stable" liquidity | Cash fell from $649M (Q1 2025) to $556M (Q1 2026); the Q2 balance of $1.034B was temporarily inflated by a new $550M 2031 note, used on 2026-07-20 to redeem the 2027 notes. Net debt (debt minus cash) is ~$1.30B ex-leases | Accurate but generous wording — the balance sheet is deliberately levered and book equity is negative |
| New registrations are "quality names" | First-time renewal rate held in the "mid-40% range"; Q2 2026 total renewal rate 75.2% vs 75.5% a year ago | Holding so far; the true test is 2026–27 when the record 2025–26 cohorts first come up for renewal at the higher price |
| Price increase is "about $0.03 a day" | Contractually allowed 7% in four of every six years; CFO says ~50% of the November rise lands in 2027 revenue, the rest in 2028 | Mechanically sound; elasticity unproven |

**Distortions to ignore:** the screener's ROE (−47%), ROIC (−12,213%) and Altman Z (−2.4) are artifacts of negative book equity created by decades of buybacks — not distress. Piotroski 9/9 is the more honest read of operating health.

**Where the story is richer than the numbers:** the "new security services" and .web have no revenue yet; management itself says .web will contribute nothing meaningful in 2026.

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory — **Rising**

- Q1 2025: cautious, "a measure of caution until the macroeconomic situation clarifies."
- Q3 2025: steady; ICANN new-domain round described as "2027 … probably the earliest."
- Q4 2025: confident — "positive trends … gained strength and continued throughout 2025."
- Q1 2026: "strong results … both operationally and financially"; record base.
- Q2 2026: the most assertive language in the set — "record," "highest rate we have seen in 20 years," "synergistic convergence" of AI and channel tailwinds.

Guidance specificity improved: ranges were narrowed each quarter rather than widened. The language moved from defensive (macro, caution) to offensive (records, new products, .web), and that shift was earned by the numbers.

## 4. Guidance credibility — **High**

- **2025 revenue guide** went $1.635–1.650B (Q1) → $1.645–1.655B (Q2) → $1.652–1.657B (Q3) → actual ~$1.66B. Delivered at or above the top end.
- **2025 domain base** guided −0.7% to +0.9% in April 2025; delivered +2.6%. Large conservative bias.
- **2026 revenue guide** $1.715–1.735B (Feb) → $1.730–1.745B (Apr) → $1.745–1.755B (Jul). Raised twice.
- **2026 domain base** 1.5–3.5% (Feb) → raised in April → 5.2–6.0% (Jul).

The screener's 57% EPS beat rate (4 of 7) understates this: the misses are small and explained (the Q4 2025 miss, $2.23 vs ~$2.35, was a one-off foreign tax charge and a real-estate impairment; Q2 2026's $2.38 was a beat on one consensus and a 4-cent miss on another). On revenue and operating income the company is a consistent sandbagger — it guides low and raises.

## 5. Analyst pressure points

- **Pull-forward ahead of the price rise.** Baird asked directly whether record registrations were buyers rushing ahead of 2026-11-01. Bidzos: "I can't say that that's not a factor … We just don't see it as anything coming close to a material factor." This is the most important unresolved question for 2027.
- **Renewal-rate dilution.** Citi asked about churn as the record cohorts age; the CFO conceded "a little bit of a tick down … in the remainder of this year and then possibly into next year."
- **Capital spending.** JPMorgan flagged memory and server cost inflation; 2026 capex guidance ($55–65M) is roughly double the usual run rate, and the CFO expects prices to "stay elevated and probably be more elevated." Small in dollars against ~$1.07B of free cash flow.
- **New products.** Asked twice (Feb and Jul) with no specifics, no pricing, no revenue timeline. A recurring non-answer.
- **Not asked on the calls (post-dates them):** the Hagens Berman antitrust class action of 2026-09-04 against VeriSign and ICANN alleging excessive .com fees.

## 6. Red flags and green flags

- Red flag (Q2 2026): new security products paused behind .web after being promised "in the coming months" in Q4 2025.
- Red flag (ongoing): returns of more than 100% of free cash flow are partly debt-funded; net debt ~$1.30B and negative equity. Comfortable at ~1.1x operating income, but it removes balance-sheet slack in a 5% ten-year-yield world.
- Red flag (2026-09-04): antitrust class action targets the core .com pricing right; this is the first fresh legal attack on the franchise in years.
- Red flag (insiders): 78 open-market sells vs 2 trivial buys; the CEO sells 3,300 shares roughly monthly (most recently 2026-09-22 at ~$304.74), consistent with a pre-planned program but never offset by buying.
- Green flag (Q1–Q2 2026): record new registrations (+14% and +21% year over year) with first-time renewals holding in the mid-40s.
- Green flag (2026-07-22): .web delegated, ending a decade-long dispute; general availability late 2026 or early 2027, with full pricing freedom and premium-name sales not possible in .com.
- Green flag (Q2 2026): buyback authorization lifted to $1.5B.
- Green flag (all quarters): 29 years of 100% uptime — the operational basis of the regulatory franchise.

## 7. Hidden signals

- **Vocabulary shift on AI:** from "certainly having some impact, but … one of several components" (Feb 2026) to "AI is definitely enhancing demand for domain names" (Jul 2026). Management now treats AI as a tailwind rather than a threat — the opposite of the market's 2025 worry that AI search would make websites (and therefore domains) less necessary.
- **.web is framed as "very different" from .com:** governed by ICANN only, not the Commerce Department contract, with "complete wholesale pricing flexibility." This is the first VeriSign asset with free pricing — strategically meaningful even if small.
- **CFO transition (May 2025):** John Calys replaced George Kilguss with no change in disclosure style or guidance conservatism — continuity is a positive.
- **Channel commentary:** repeated emphasis on an "evolving" registrar channel (M&A, website builders becoming registrars). VeriSign's largest customer is GoDaddy; channel concentration is a quiet dependency.

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict (for the director)

**Trajectory: strengthening.** Unit growth went from contraction to ~5% inside two years, pricing power resumes on 2026-11-01, and every dollar of surplus cash is returned.

**The single most important thing to weigh:** this is a high-quality business priced close to fair value. At $291.70 the stock trades at roughly 31.6x TTM EPS and ~25x free cash flow, which already embeds the domain acceleration and the price rise. The excess return from here depends on the 2027 renewal cohorts holding up after the price increase, not on anything the market has missed.

**Moat:** a regulatory-license moat, reinforced by switching costs (changing a .com address is not practical for an established business). Width is wide: gross margin is stable at 88%, operating margin ~68%, and free cash flow growing (+22% in 2025). The negative ROIC is an accounting artifact of negative equity, not erosion. Trend: stable — margins are flat-to-slightly-up and unit growth is accelerating.

**Secular threat:** manageable. AI-driven search was the feared terminal threat in 2024–25; the 2026 data point the other way (record registrations). The real structural risk is regulatory — the Commerce Department contract, ICANN, and now an antitrust class action — which could cap future pricing but does not shrink the base. The current price is neither a fear-driven discount nor a value trap; it is a fair price for a durable franchise.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory improving · a wide, durable moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.

# VeriSign (VRSN) - a deep dive on management and the setup
*Debate run 2026-10-12. Live price $304.04 (NASDAQ, US dollars, FMP quote 2026-10-12). Transcripts covered: Q2 2025 (2025-07-24) through Q2 2026 (2026-07-23).*

**The short version:** VeriSign is a regulated near-monopoly (it runs the .com and .net registries under contracts with ICANN, the body that coordinates internet names, and the US Commerce Department) whose story got better, not worse, over the last five quarters. Domain-name growth went from "stabilising" to "accelerating", guidance was raised at every call, and management did what it said. The numbers corroborate the words. The open questions are not about honesty; they are about price (the stock trades near its 52-week high) and a new antitrust class action filed 2026-09-04.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC
- **Q2 2025 (2025-07-24):** the message was a turn in the channel. Registrars (the retail sellers such as GoDaddy) had "refocused on customer acquisition" and were engaging with VeriSign's marketing programmes. The domain base guide for 2025 was raised to growth of 1.2%-2% after years of shrinkage.
- **Q3 2025 (2025-10-23):** the guide rose again to 2.2%-2.5%. .web (a new top-level domain VeriSign has fought to operate for a decade) was still in an ICANN review, with a final hearing set for mid-November 2025.
- **Q4 2025 (2026-02-05):** 2025 closed with 41.7 million new registrations (the most since 2021), a base of 173.5 million names (+2.6%) and the first dividend year. 2026 guidance: base growth 1.5%-3.5%, revenue $1.715-1.735 billion. Capital spending roughly doubled to $55-65 million because server and memory prices are being pushed up by AI data-centre demand.
- **Q1 2026 (2026-04-23):** record base of 176.1 million; base guide raised to 3.1%-4.x%; revenue guide raised to $1.730-1.745 billion. Management gave notice of the first allowed .com price increase in two years: $10.26 to $10.97 wholesale (about 6.9%) effective 2026-11-01.
- **Q2 2026 (2026-07-23):** record 12.7 million new registrations, base 179.1 million, base guide raised again to 5.2%-6%, revenue guide to $1.745-1.755 billion. .web was delegated into the root zone with VeriSign as operator, but guidance assumes no meaningful .web revenue. A new, AI-security product line was trailed ("you won't have to wait too much longer"). Buyback authority topped up to $1.5 billion.

The arc is expansion: from "the base has stopped shrinking" to "the base is growing at the fastest rate in years, a price increase is coming, and .web is ours". Nothing was quietly dropped.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)
| Management claim | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Base growth is accelerating | 173.5M (end-2025) -> 176.1M (Q1) -> 179.1M (Q2 2026); +3.05M in Q2 alone | Corroborated |
| Revenue growth steady in the mid-single digits | 2025 revenue $1.66B, +6.4%; Q1 2026 +6.6%; Q2 2026 +6.0%; 3-year CAGR +5.2% | Corroborated |
| "Sound financial discipline" | Gross margin 88.2% stable; free-cash-flow margin about 64%; trailing twelve-month free cash flow $1.07B | Corroborated |
| Operating margin "more consistent with long-term trend" in 2026 | Q2 2026 operating expense $138M vs $121M a year earlier (+14%), faster than revenue (+6%); operating income +5.6% | Corroborated - margin is drifting down slightly, exactly as flagged |
| Returning more than 100% of free cash flow | $1.17B returned in the year to Q2 2026 vs about $1.07B free cash flow; funded partly by debt (net debt $1.31B at 2026-06-30; $550M 2027 notes refinanced with 5.1% 2031 notes) | Corroborated, with leverage creeping up |
| EPS growth well ahead of revenue | 2025 EPS $8.81, +10.1%; trailing EPS $9.22; latest quarter +8% | Corroborated - buybacks do the work |

The story is not richer than the numbers. If anything, management under-promises on .web and on pricing.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY - Rising
- Q2 2025: cautious optimism, "improving channel trends".
- Q4 2025: "the positive domain name-based trends ... gained strength and continued throughout 2025".
- Q2 2026: "strong results ... both operationally and financially"; "the factors driving the solid domain name base trends ... accelerated". The CEO also links AI tools ("making content and website creation faster and easier") to new registrations - turning a feared threat into a stated tailwind.
Language stays offensive (growth, new products, .web) rather than defensive. The only defensive notes are cost-side: memory and server inflation (Q4 2025, Q2 2026) and legal costs (Q3 2025).

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY - High
- 2025 revenue guide of $1.652-1.657B (Q3 2025) delivered at $1.66B.
- 2025 base guide raised twice and met.
- 2026 revenue guide raised at both Q1 and Q2; base guide raised from 1.5%-3.5% to 5.2%-6%.
The 57% quarterly EPS beat rate in the screener understates reliability: VeriSign guides revenue and operating income narrowly and rarely misses those; EPS "misses" mostly reflect tax-rate noise (for example the Q4 2025 foreign tax charge). Mild sandbagging pattern on the domain base.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS
- **Renewal rates after the price increase.** Asked in Q1 and Q2 2026. Management concedes a "tick down" as first-time renewals grow (Q2 2026 rate 75.2% vs 75.5% a year earlier) and that the outcome depends on registrar retail pricing. This is the most important unanswered question for 2027.
- **.web costs and revenue.** Repeatedly asked; management will not size it.
- **Capital spending beyond 2026.** Management said prices are "going to stay elevated and probably be more elevated" and declined to guide 2027.
- **.net pricing.** Allowed up to 10% a year; no increase announced (Q1 2026) - optionality left unused.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS
Red flags:
- Persistent open-market selling by the CEO (for example 3,300 shares on 2026-09-22 at about $304.74 and another 3,300 sold at about $296.58 reported 2026-09-29); 2 open-market buys versus 78 sells over the period. Routine and small relative to his 385,027 directly held shares, but there is no insider buying at all.
- Operating expense growth (+14% year on year in Q2 2026) outpacing revenue; capital spending doubled on AI-driven hardware inflation.
- Leverage rising to fund payouts above free cash flow; negative shareholder equity (hence the misleading negative Altman Z-score and ROE - these reflect buybacks, not distress).
- New antitrust class action (Hagens Berman, filed 2026-09-04) alleging excessive .com fees.
Green flags:
- Record new registrations in Q2 2026 (12.7M) and a base guide raised from 1.5%-3.5% to 5.2%-6% in two quarters.
- 29 years of 100% resolution availability; first contractual price increase since 2024 locked in for 2026-11-01.
- .web delegated (Q2 2026) at near-zero guided cost.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS
- The vocabulary shifted from "registry" to "high assurance critical infrastructure" and "Zero Trust" security for an "agentic AI world" (Q2 2026). Management is preparing investors for a second product line - the first real diversification attempt in a decade.
- CFO John Calys gave unusually explicit modelling help on the price increase (about half of the November increase lands in 2027 revenue, the rest in 2028), suggesting confidence in the 2027-28 revenue path.
- AI is now framed as a demand driver, not a threat - a meaningful rhetorical change from the 2024 "generative AI and search" worries.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)
**Trajectory: stable to strengthening.** The single most important thing to weigh: this is a superb franchise priced as one. At $304 it trades at about 26 times free cash flow, roughly in line with the analysts' own fair value; the return from here is mostly the earnings growth (high single digits plus buybacks), not a re-rating.

**Moat:** regulatory licence. Width is wide: 88% gross margins held flat through the 2021-22 inflation, returns on invested capital are extreme and not falling, and the contracts grant price rises (up to 7% a year on .com in the back four years of each six-year window). Trend is stable. **Secular threat:** manageable - AI-driven discovery could in theory reduce the need for memorable domain names, but the 2026 data show the opposite (record registrations), and the bigger tail risk is regulatory (the antitrust suit, or a future contract renewal that removes pricing rights). The cheapness question does not arise: this is not cheap, so it is neither a fear-print nor a value trap.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory steady · a wide, durable moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.

# VeriSign (VRSN) - a deep dive on management and the setup
*Prepared 2026-10-19 from five earnings calls (Q2 2025 through Q2 2026, the latest on 2026-07-23) and the screener's financial trajectory. Price context: last close $302.34 on 2026-10-16. The third-quarter 2026 report is due 2026-10-22, after the close.*

**Bottom line:** VeriSign is a regulated toll road on the internet's most-used address suffixes, .com and .net. Across the last five calls the story got better, and the numbers moved with it: guidance for growth in the number of registered names was raised at every call, from roughly flat in mid-2025 to 5.2%-6.0% for 2026, and earnings per share (EPS) rose about 10% a year. Management is unusually terse, but what it says lines up with what it reports. The open questions are not about honesty; they are about how much of the recent surge in new registrations is promotion-driven and will churn out, and how much a near-monopoly growing revenue at about 6% a year should cost.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

- **Q2 2025 (2025-07-24):** a recovery story. After two years of a shrinking name base, management raised its 2025 base-growth guidance and stressed "some conservatism as economic and geopolitical uncertainty exists". The big open item was .web, a new suffix VeriSign won at auction in 2016 but which was tied up in disputes; Jim Bidzos (executive chairman and CEO) called the opponent's use of ICANN (the internet's naming authority) processes "an abuse of process".
- **Q3 2025 (2025-10-23):** recovery confirmed. Free cash flow (FCF, the cash left after running the business and investing in it) of $303 million versus $248 million a year earlier; management first named increasing use of AI as "a primary driver" of rising registration and query activity.
- **Q4 2025 (2026-02-05):** 41.7 million new registrations in 2025, the most since 2021; the base grew to 173.5 million names. An impairment charge sat in the quarter.
- **Q1 2026 (2026-04-23):** the base reached 176.1 million; the renewal rate (share of names renewed when due) of 76.3% was later called the highest in 20 years; the company gave notice of a 6.9% .com wholesale price rise, from $10.26 to $10.97, effective 2026-11-01. A new thread appeared: security products built on VeriSign's infrastructure.
- **Q2 2026 (2026-07-23):** a record 12.7 million new registrations; base guidance raised to 5.2%-6.0%; .web finally delegated into the root zone (the master directory of suffixes), with a launch planned for late 2026 and no meaningful 2026 revenue; buyback authorization topped up to $1.5 billion; a $550 million 4.75% note due 2027 refinanced with a 5.1% note due 2031.

The arc moved from defending a flat base to describing accelerating demand plus two new options (.web and security services). Nothing was quietly dropped: the AI tailwind, the marketing programs and the buyback have been constant themes.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS

| Management claim | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Strong, sustained domain demand | Revenue $1.33B (2021) to $1.66B (2025), about 5% a year; Q2 2026 revenue +6% y/y; 2026 guide $1.745-1.755B (+5.5-6%) | Matches |
| Pricing plus volume drive earnings | EPS $7.00 (2021) to $8.81 (2025); trailing-twelve-month (TTM) diluted EPS $9.22; Q2 2026 EPS +7.7% | Matches; EPS growth is helped by a shrinking share count |
| More than 100% of FCF returned | TTM returns $1.17B against TTM FCF of about $1.07B; net debt rose to about $1.31B (borrowings $2.33B less cash $1.03B, at 2026-06-30) | Matches, but the gap is funded with debt, and the new note costs 5.1% versus 4.75% |
| Margins are durable | Gross margin 88.2%, stable; FCF margin about 64%; operating margin about 68% | Matches |
| Operating costs are contained | Q2 2026 operating expense $138M versus $121M a year earlier (+14%), faster than revenue (+6%); operating income +5.6% | Richer story than numbers: costs are now growing faster than sales, partly marketing programs and partly memory and server inflation flagged on the call |
| AI is a tailwind | Record registrations coincide with the AI build-out, but management cannot separate AI-driven demand from registrar promotions | Plausible, not proven |

Accounting distortions to note: book equity is negative because buybacks exceeded retained earnings, which makes return on equity (-47%) and the Altman Z solvency score (-2.2) meaningless here; return on invested capital (ROIC) of over 3,000% reflects a business that needs almost no capital.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rising.** Q2 2025 hedged with "some conservatism"; Q3 2025 described "solid underlying demand"; Q1 2026 said the positive trends "continued to build strength"; Q2 2026 said the drivers "accelerated" and called the quarter's registrations "the largest we have seen for any quarter in our history". Guidance became both higher and narrower each quarter. The tone moved to offense (new products, .web) without abandoning the core message of reliability (29 years of 100% availability). One defensive note crept in on Q2 2026: capital spending pressure from memory and server prices that "are going to stay elevated and probably be more elevated".

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

Base-growth guidance went from around flat-to-modest in mid-2025, to 3.1%-4.3% (2026-04-23), to 5.2%-6.0% (2026-07-23); revenue guidance from $1.730-1.745B to $1.745-1.755B; operating income from $1.170-1.185B to $1.185-1.195B. Every revision was upward, which suggests a habit of guiding conservatively. The screener's beat rate (4 of 7 quarters, 57%) is lower than that pattern implies, because the sell side models the same visible daily base data the company publishes; misses are small. **Reliability: High.**

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **Renewal quality after the registration surge.** Asked repeatedly (Citi, Q1 and Q2 2026). The chief financial officer, John Calys, concedes "a little bit of a tick down" in renewals as first-time renewing names grow as a share, into 2027. This is the most important unresolved question: promotion-heavy cohorts renew at lower rates.
- **Elasticity to the November price rise.** Management says $10.97 a year is "about $0.03 a day"; true for most users, but registrar retail markups decide the real effect, and VeriSign does not control them.
- **Registrar promotional intensity, especially at GoDaddy, the largest customer.** Bidzos answered at length without quantifying how much volume is promotion-driven (Q1 2026). A non-answer.
- **.web costs and timing; long-term AI risk to the open web.** Answered: .web costs are inside guidance; AI is framed as a positive.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

Red:
- Operating expense growing faster than revenue in Q2 2026 (+14% versus +6%).
- Q2 2026 renewal rate of 75.2% slipped from 75.5% a year earlier, with management guiding to further softness as large new cohorts come due.
- Insiders: 78 open-market sales (50,450 shares) versus 2 tiny buys - routine for a mature company with large equity grants, but no insider is buying at these prices.
- Buybacks above FCF are adding debt at higher interest rates.

Green:
- Record new registrations (Q2 2026) and a 20-year-high renewal rate (Q1 2026).
- Contractual pricing: the 6.9% .com increase from 2026-11-01 flows into revenue mostly in 2027 (about half) and 2028; a .net wholesale price rise was also announced around late August 2026.
- .web delegated (2026-07-22) after a decade of disputes - a free option.
- Buyback capacity of $1.5 billion with no expiry.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- The phrase "high assurance" appeared in Q1 2026 and became the anchor of the new-product story; the promised blog series was delayed by a quarter (Q2 2026 admitted the rollout was "paused"). A small slip on a self-imposed timeline.
- Management now speaks of a channel that is "diverse and evolving" - website builders turning into registrars - which hints at less dependence on GoDaddy, but also at more promotion-driven volume.
- CFO candor on revenue timing: only about half of the price rise lands in 2027 revenue. That makes 2027 growth more predictable, and reduces the scope for a surprise.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT

**Trajectory: strengthening.** Demand, pricing and capital returns all moved the right way across the five calls, with management's words confirmed by the numbers.

**The single most important thing to weigh:** the price, not the business. At $302 the company is valued at about 27 times trailing FCF (enterprise value of roughly $29 billion including net debt), close to its 52-week high, for revenue growth of about 6% and EPS growth of about 10%. The upcoming price rise is already known and modeled by the sell side.

**Moat:** a regulatory license (the exclusive .com/.net registry contracts with ICANN and the US Commerce Department) combined with switching costs on the user side (a business cannot easily move its address). Returns and margins are stable at extreme levels - an 88% gross margin, unchanged - so the moat is wide and stable, not eroding. The same regulation caps pricing, which keeps growth modest.

**Secular threat:** manageable. AI could in principle reduce the need to type web addresses, but today the evidence points the other way (record registrations and query volume). The real long-run risks are regulatory: price-cap terms in future contract renewals and new suffix competition from ICANN's 2026 application round. Neither impairs terminal value on present evidence. The stock is not cheap because of fear; it is fairly valued because it is good.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC
A year ago (Q3-2025) the story was a toll road coming back to life: the .com/.net base had stopped shrinking and management credited registrar marketing programs. Through 2026 the story widened in three steps:

VeriSign Informed, a certificate-revocation checking service, was announced 2026-10-05, with pricing by year-end and availability in the first half of 2027.
Nothing was quietly dropped. The one shift is that the call now spends real time on unproven new products; the core story is unchanged.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)
| Claim | Evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Strong results" in Q3-2026 | Revenue $443M, +5.7% y/y; operating income $296M, +4.2%; EPS $2.35 vs $2.27 (+3.5%; +6% excluding a $0.06 held-for-sale write-down) | Solid, not strong. Revenue growth is tracking the domain base, operating income lags it. |
